synopsis: X-in-the-loop is a ladder from all-virtual toward all-real testing: expanding the real-system boundary from software to ECU, sensor and complete machine exposes additional failure modes but increases complexity and sacrifices speed, scalability, controllability and test volume [f13311, f5227, f13321]. The recommended allocation is MIL/SIL for high-volume early testing, HIL for real-controller timing, interfaces and faults, selective VIL where added fidelity warrants investment, and real machines for stopping, terrain and environmental effects; these methods complement rather than replace one another [f13313, f13314, f13315, f5743]. The pipeline should operate under continuous integration with automatic pass criteria and proving-ground anchors, with a versioned scenario library, SIL/HIL suite, statistical acceptance plan and correlated machine-dynamics models ideally ready by mid-2027 [f7142, f7141, f5616]. Engineering simulation can find defects and tune thresholds before machines exist, but the cited Daimler Truck India and HCLTech examples demonstrate engineering development rather than external safety acceptance; ISO 19014-4's 2020 edition contains normative Annex B on software validation test environments [f1447, f1449, f10532]. Commercial IPG offerings have direct off-highway MIL/SIL/HIL/VIL relevance, but documented sensor-stimulated VIL is limited to road vehicles, a 2024 road-vehicle survey reports high cost and varying accuracy, and no end-to-end heavy off-road automatic-braking VIL case was found [f8807, f13318, f13319, f13320].

relations.note: Both describe broader real-system boundaries exposing failures while reducing testing efficiency and control.
Both recommend continuous integration and automatic pass criteria across the validation pipeline.
Both identify IPG's off-highway MIL, SIL, HIL and VIL capabilities.
The boundary-based method identifies the specific components progressively replacing simulation.
Automotive literature supports organizing tests by the real-system boundary.
Published on-road work illustrates the progression toward increasingly real testing.
Different boundaries explain complementary uncertainty reduction and extend the list to replay and sensors.
Documented programmes combine methods, consistent with their complementary roles.
Allocation separates decision correctness, safe execution and perception correctness.
Glossary adds controller checks and closed-loop braking to the proving-ground anchor recommendation.
Thousands of nightly MIL/SIL cases quantify the automated pipeline's intended volume.
Fidelity-versus-efficiency tradeoffs justify selective VIL and high-volume SIL.
Reported VIL cost and variable accuracy support requiring investment justification.
Pre-machine defect detection supports reserving prototype hours for uniquely physical phenomena.
Engineering simulation addresses testing before final hardware exists.
Building the planned SIL/HIL capability requires simulation, interface, timing and fault-injection expertise.
Off-highway VIL availability contrasts with absent end-to-end braking evidence; capability is not validation.
Road-only sensor-stimulation documentation reinforces the heavy off-road VIL evidence gap.
